pll1d31c4-d1e3501.summary: States that the three are rightly called 'one thing' (unum) and one God, but not 'one' (unus). Several things can be called one thing if of one essence and nature; 'unus' or 'una' cannot be said of diverse things unless one adds 'one what,' with which it can be said of things of one or diverse substances.
claims: The three are 'unum' and one God, but not 'unus.'
'One' with a qualifier can apply to things of different substance.

pll1d31c4-d1e3504.summary: Cites De Trinitate VI: Scripture never says things of diverse nature 'are one,' and things of one nature that disagree are not one in that respect. 'One' without qualification signifies the same nature and essence, not dissenting.
claims: 'One' without qualification signifies same nature and agreement.

pll1d31c4-d1e3523.summary: Continues Augustine: Paul and Apollos, both men and agreeing, are 'one.' With a qualifier, things of different natures can be one, as soul and body are one man, and 'he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit,' since man's spirit becomes one with God by sharing his truth and beatitude. If so, much more are those of one substance one God.
claims: Soul and body are one man.
One who cleaves to God is one spirit with him.
Much more are Father and Son one God.

pll1d31c4-d1e3572.summary: Notes that this condemns the Arian heresy, which denies that Father, Son, and Spirit are of one ousia and makes the Son a creature, and the Sabellian, which makes Christ the same as Father and Spirit, a trinity of names without subsisting persons.
claims: Arianism denies one essence and makes the Son a creature.
Sabellianism makes a trinity of names without subsisting persons.

pll1d31c4-d1e3589.summary: Cites Augustine on John: Truth crushes both heresies with 'I and the Father are one.' 'One' frees from Arius, 'are' from Sabellius; if one, not diverse; if 'are,' Father and Son. Sabellians (Patripassians) confuse the persons; Arians make two substances, greater and lesser. Sail between: the Father is Father and the Son Son, other but not another thing.
claims: 'One' refutes Arius; 'are' refutes Sabellius.
Father and Son are alius but not aliud.

pll1d31c4-d1e3644.summary: Concludes that it has been shown why unity is said to be in the Father, since the three are one.
claims: Unity is attributed to the Father though the three are one.

pll1d31c4-d1e3649.summary: Cites Hilary, De Synodis: the synod's 'three by substance, one by consonance' may seem to speak less expressly of the likeness of Father and Son, but it meant to destroy the impiety that reduced the three to names of one Father. They said three substances to teach subsisting persons, not to separate the substance by dissimilar essence. 'One by consonance' is not blameworthy because, with the Spirit named, unity of consonance was fitting.
claims: The synod spoke of three substances to affirm subsisting persons.
It did not separate the essence by dissimilarity.

pll1d31c4-d1e3669.summary: Further Hilary: confessing God the Father and Christ the Son of God without professing two gods, they must be one in the kind of essence, since their essence can have only one name. Unity of name does not deprive the begotten essence of being a person, as if a single solitary substance were meant, but one God is predicated because of the undifferentiated nature in both.
claims: Father and Son are one God by undifferentiated nature.
Unity of name does not abolish the person of the Son.

pl-l1d31c4.summary: Explains that Father, Son, and Spirit are rightly called 'one' (unum) and one God, but not 'one' in the masculine (unus). With Augustine, things are called 'unum' without qualification only when of one nature and agreeing, as Paul and Apollos are one; when 'what one' is added, things of diverse natures can be one, as soul and body one man, or one who cleaves to the Lord one spirit with him. So much more are those of one substance one God. This condemns the Arians (different substance, the Son a creature) and Sabellians (one person, a trinity of names); Augustine on John 10:30: 'one' frees you from Arius, 'are' from Sabellius; sail between Scylla and Charybdis. Hilary, De Synodis, explains that 'three by substance, one by consonance' meant subsisting persons, not separate essences, and that the persons are one God by an undifferentiated nature.
claims: The three are rightly called 'one thing' and one God, but not 'one person.'
'Unum' without qualification signifies one nature and agreement.
With a qualifier, things of different natures can be called one.
If one who cleaves to God is one spirit with him, much more are the persons one God.
'One' in John 10:30 refutes Arius; 'are' refutes Sabellius.
Three substances in the sense of three subsisting persons do not imply different essences.
